Triggers.value: The same time of day the event occurred

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

vignette:
Leilani, at 66, had owned "Island Treasures," her small shop filled with imported crafts and fabrics, for nearly twenty years. It had been her anchor after her divorce, a place of quiet purpose. Now, it felt like a cage. She came to therapy because the world, and her own mind, had begun to feel profoundly unsafe. The precipitating event was a police raid on her business nine months prior, a case of mistaken identity that had been violent, chaotic, and humiliating.

The raid happened late one Tuesday afternoon, just as she was preparing to close. The memory itself is a collection of searing, disjointed fragments. She can’t put the experience into words; trying to describe it feels like grabbing at smoke. What remains is the feeling of being watched by the officers lining the wall, the sudden, disorienting dizziness as she was shoved against a counter, and the impenetrable darkness of the stockroom where she was held. There are parts of the event she simply cannot remember, blank spaces where the worst of it must have happened. This fractured, unreal quality of the memory has become a source of profound distress, convincing her that something is fundamentally wrong with her mind. She has come to believe that her inability to recall the event coherently means she is a "lousy coper," or worse, that she is going crazy. This fear makes her recoil from the memory fragments whenever they surface, which only ensures they remain unprocessed and terrifyingly incomplete.

These fragments are no longer confined to the past. The triggers are everywhere, especially in the shop that was once her sanctuary. As the clock nears 4:30 PM each day, the time the raid occurred, a familiar lightheadedness begins to set in. If a customer lingers too long, their gaze feels like a hostile observation, and the dizziness returns with a sickening lurch. These moments instantly plunge her back into the wordless horror of the event, the memory replaying not as a story but as a pure bodily sensation. The recurrence of these physical reactions has cemented her belief that she is inadequate, unable to handle the normal demands of her life. This conviction, in turn, makes her hyper-aware of being watched, interpreting any neutral glance from a customer as a sign of judgment on her visible fragility.

To manage this escalating terror, Leilani’s world has shrunk dramatically. The daily wave of late-afternoon dizziness, and the cascade of fragmented memories it brings, led her to start closing the shop hours early. This avoidance of the circumstances of the trauma has had devastating financial consequences, which only reinforces her self-appraisal as an inadequate failure. To soothe the intense anxiety that now pervades her evenings, she has fallen into a pattern of compulsive online spending, buying expensive items she neither wants nor needs. The brief distraction gives way to crushing shame, further proof of her inability to cope. This cycle of avoidance and distraction has kept the traumatic memory perfectly preserved in its most toxic form; by never allowing herself to be in a triggering situation long enough to see that she might survive it, she keeps the memory’s power intact and her negative beliefs unchallenged.

The connections have now formed a devastatingly efficient feedback loop. Her strategy of avoiding the shop in the late afternoon has made that time of day an even more potent trigger, a clear demarcation of when her safety ends. When a memory fragment does break through—a flash of the stockroom’s darkness—it triggers an immediate, desperate need to escape, compelling her to avoid the upcoming anniversary of the raid at all costs. This avoidance validates her belief that she is too weak to handle it, a lousy coper who must hide from her own life. The shame from this belief then fuels another late-night spending spree, a maladaptive strategy that further isolates her and deepens her conviction that she is spiraling out of control.

Leilani sought help after receiving a final notice on her shop’s lease, a direct consequence of the lost revenue from her truncated hours. She sat in the office, her hands trembling slightly, and confessed her deepest fear. It wasn't just about losing the shop; it was the terrifying, quiet belief that her reactions were not a temporary response to trauma, but proof that her mind was irrevocably breaking.
